newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Nervous Albanian capital empties amid gunfire.
newsitem.headline: Nervous Albanian capital empties amid gunfire.

text.p: Housewives bustled through Tirana's nervous streets on Thursday, stocking up on butter, cooking oil and eggs and trying hard not to notice crackles of gunfire.

By mid-afternoon, the city centre was emptied and eerie. Residents braced for a rampage by mobs brandishing weapons stolen from army depots -- the scenes in other Albanian towns and cities they had been watch for more than a week on Italian or German television piped into most Tirana homes.
The profusion of cafes occupying what was a park covering two large blocks in Communist times were closed up tight, their mostly male clientele nowhere to be seen.
The truckloads of police deployed in and around central Skanderbeg Square for weeks to deter demonstrations against President Sali Berisha were also gone.
In Tirana, as in southern Albania for the past two weeks, authority had crumbled.
As dusk fell, tracer bullets lit up a starry sky, though no one knew why they had been fired or where they came from.
Volley after volley of automatic fire pierced the night -- all but halted after the appearance on a central tree-lined boulevard of two tanks.
But it was by day that the nervousness of Tirana residents was apparent.
Most small food shops were open but large crowds, made up mostly of women, milled around and chatted outside bakeries with no bread to sell.
Shoppers scurried through the streets, gingerly carrying trays of eggs or plastic bags bulging with late purchases.
One butcher shop had nothing but minced beef on offer.
"How about some fillet steak?" asked the owner, gesturing to a cellar underneath the shop, where he kept back prime meat for customers with enough cash to pay for it.
Market stalls normally jammed with mid-day customers were closed and owners of smart boutiques selling goods beyond the budget of most Albanians put up reinforced shutters.
Owners packed up inventories, shoved them into car boots and drove them away for safe keeping elsewhere.
Would-be passengers briefly besieged airline offices, closed along with Tirana's dilapidated Rinas airport.
Small groups of elderly men sat playing cards in a rubbish-strewn park, apparently oblivious to the tension.
A 30-strong crowd broke into a run down a rubbish-filled side street -- pushing and shoving their way into a minibus barely after it had stopped.

"That's going to Elbasan," a man in his 60s said, referring to a town in central Albania where returning journalists said rebels finally seized power on Thursday. "The fare's about the same as a dollar."
A tidy sum in Europe's poorest country, where average salaries are less than $80 and many earn far less.

Albanians exposed to more than a month of violence heard repeatedly broadcast appeals from the new prime minister, local officials and Moslem, Orthodox and Roman Catholic clergy to remain calm and not panic.
But one television newsreader issued a heartfelt appeal of her own as she cast down her pen and notes.

"As a citizen and mother who has spoken to you for so many years, it's not easy to read news so tragic for my country," she said. "Let's say no to killing our brothers, no to bloodshed. All of us together for this Albania, so small and poor but so dear to all of us.
